methods.label: Compare magnitudes and arguments
methods.explanation:
The number \(a-bi\) is the conjugate of \(a+bi\), so polar form separates the equation into conditions on magnitude and direction. Set \(z=a+bi\) and \(\overline z=a-bi\). Each complex number \(z\) determines exactly one ordered pair \((a,b)\).

First, \(z=0\) works. For \(z\ne0\), write
\[
z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta),\qquad r>0,\quad 0\le\theta<2\pi.
\]
Conjugation preserves magnitude and reverses the argument. Taking an integer power raises the magnitude to that power and multiplies the argument by the exponent. Therefore \(z^{2002}=\overline z\) is equivalent to
\[
r^{2002}=r,\qquad 2002\theta=-\theta+2\pi k
\]
for some integer \(k\). Dividing the magnitude equation by \(r>0\) gives \(r^{2001}=1\), so \(r=1\). The argument equation gives
\[
\theta=\frac{2\pi k}{2003}.
\]
The restriction \(0\le\theta<2\pi\) permits exactly \(k=0,1,\ldots,2002\). Every one of these angles satisfies the original equation, and they give distinct complex numbers because their directions are distinct within one full turn. These are the \(2003\)rd roots of unity.

None is zero, so including the separate solution \(z=0\) gives \(2003+1=\boxed{2004}\) ordered pairs, choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
